hook.line: Talking about money means comparing, and English uses "than" for everything. Spanish has two ways to say it, and choosing the wrong one sounds off even when people understand you.
hook.es: Gana más de lo que dice.
hook.en: He earns more than he says.

examples.es: Gana más de lo que dice.
examples.en: He earns more than he says.
You work more than Vale. (to a friend)

examples.es: Trabajas más de lo que crees.
examples.en: You work more than you think. (to a friend)

examples.es: Es más caro que el otro.
examples.en: It's more expensive than the other one.

examples.es: Es más caro de lo que pensaba.
examples.en: It's more expensive than I thought.

rule:
Ask what comes after "than".

A person, thing or number: *más que*.
*Gana más que yo.* *Es más caro que el otro.*

A verb with its own subject (a whole thought): *más de lo que*.
*Gana más de lo que dice.* *Es más caro de lo que pensaba.*

A quick test: can you add a verb in English? "Than me" is just a person, so *que yo*. "Than he says" has a verb, so *de lo que*.

Same with *menos*.
smallPrint: Teachers call the first a comparison of nouns and the second a comparison with a clause.

pitfalls.right: Gana más de lo que dice.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Before a verb, Spanish adds *de lo*.

pitfalls.wrong: Gana más de lo que yo.
pitfalls.why: A bare person after "than" only needs *que*.

pitfalls.wrong: Es más caro de lo el otro.
pitfalls.right: Es más caro que el otro.
pitfalls.why: *El otro* is a thing, not a clause, so just *que*.

personal: Compare yourself with a friend using *más que*, then say something about yourself with *más de lo que* (for example, how much you sleep or work).
